definition: A proof task states a success criterion when it tells the learner something falsifiable about the result: a value to compare theirs against, a conditional test, or an instruction to predict before looking. A statement of why the task matters, or of what its output means whatever the output is, does not count.
method: Two independent random samples of proof tasks, labelled by hand against the definition above before any classifier was written. Sample A was used to design the patterns; sample B was labelled first and then used once, as a held-out check. The task text is frozen here on purpose: this is the known answer the classifier is scored against, so it must not move when the corpus does.

A-tuned-on.task: Run the golden path, especially step 3. A conflict over non-overlapping edits is the most persuasive thing in this category.

Count the interruptions before and after. Ask the expert, a month later, whether the question stopped. That number is the whole argument, and it is what NVIDIA means by "measurable reductions in support load".
Write the owner table. Four rows is enough, and a page that cannot be traced to a person has no lifecycle.
Take your last ten support tickets and label each as content gap, retrieval gap, or not a documentation problem. Ten is enough to discover which of the three you have been assuming.
Run the golden path. Step 3 is the part worth your time: watch the canonical term match inside its own variants.
Run the golden path. Step 3 is the whole point, and seeing your own build fail on a rename is more persuasive than any description of it.
Find an exercise that never says what it produced, and write that sentence. It is the fastest way to discover an exercise that produces nothing.
Generate your ground truth in CI. Parse --help, read git tags, export the glossary. The audit is only as good as the facts, and hand-maintained facts are the first thing to rot.
Point the extractor at a docs site you own and just execute the blocks. Whatever fails first is a page currently lying to readers.

Find something to retire. Pages with no views in six months, or documentation for a version out of support. Propose it with the costs from the table above, including the retrieval-competition argument.
Name the artifacts on the route whose owners' CI excludes the route. That list is a risk register nobody has written, and presenting it is a stronger demonstration of product ownership than any page.
Time the first request after a restart against the hundredth. The ratio decides whether autoscaling is viable, and it is rarely documented.
Run the one-line check against a real documentation site. curl it and count words without JavaScript. On a client-rendered site the number is near zero, and that is a two-minute finding.
Put it in CI on a golden set. The checker plus twenty question-and-expected-source pairs, failing the build when the grounded rate drops. That is the step from a script to a gate.
Take any latency claim in your own documentation and work out whether it could be true while the system fails a third of the time. If the claim is a mean or a median, it can.
Check whether a sample that times anything reads the simulation clock or the system clock. Under a simulator that can pause, the difference is not subtle.
Open your own docs workflow and count the definitions of "the checks". If the answer is two, you have the drift.
Convert the five most important of those to [text][symbol] form and turn on --strict. Whatever fails was already broken.
Pin the model version and write down why. One line in a README about a model update invalidating a stored index demonstrates operational understanding that most candidates lack.
Write down why your quickstart is or is not pinned. The written reason is the deliverable; most projects have the state without the decision.
Grep a Markdown corpus for <!--. That count is the size of your MDX migration's first obstacle.
Compute grounded@k for k of 1, 3, 5 and 10 on a corpus you own. Predict where it plateaus. The plateau tells you whether to buy a reranker or write two sentences, and that is a budget decision.
Count how many of those routes your CI actually tests. The answer is one.

Build the proposal pipeline from the golden path against a real corpus, with a real term list. Measure how many proposals a reviewer accepts; if it is above 95 percent your filter is too loose and the review is theatre.
Add the scheduling or framework overhead to one published cost figure. On an idle machine it was a third again here, and readers budget with the number you give them.
Write the two-column table above for a product you know. The disagreements about which column a page belongs in are the valuable part.
Take your most confident claim about your documentation and work out which half of analytics could test it. If it is neither, it is an assertion.
Print coverage and value distribution for every field in your corpus. Heavy skew toward one value usually means a default is being written somewhere.
Measure the per-page maximum sentence length on your docs, then read the three worst sentences out loud. The measurement takes five minutes and the reading is what convinces anybody.
Grep your corpus for ~~ and - [ ] outside code fences. If you find any, they are shipping as literal characters right now.
Write one substitution rule for a term your own project gets wrong, and run it over your existing docs. The first real finding is your evidence.
Take the thing colleagues ask you most often and write its branches. Not the procedure, the questions.
Run the golden path. Step 3 is the point, and the trap generalises past Vale.
Tag your existing samples with what they teach, then rank your support topics by volume. The gap is your backlog, and it will not look like your roadmap.
Run the golden path, including both failure cases. The typo case is the demonstration: same input, opposite outcome depending on the direction of the logic.
Take the cases still failing at k=10 and look for the reader's word on the page. In mine, both were synonyms the corpus never used.
Follow your own tutorial in a fresh environment and note the first point at which you could tell it was working. That number is the one readers feel.
Time your build with your theme and again with the default theme. The ratio tells you where your build minutes actually go.
Run the route count over your own quickstart. If it is above about 4, you have found your next piece of work.
Add a documents: field to twenty pages in a repository you own and run the comparison. Whatever it flags has been wrong for a while.

B-held-out.task: Run the golden path. The valuable part is step 5, where a reasonable structure turns out to hide failures.
Run the golden path. Steps 2 and 3 are both surprises, and step 3 is the one to remember.
Label twenty real pages for one defect type. One type, by hand, with notes. An hour, and it is the only artifact on this page that cannot be faked.
Grep for readers of your most important metadata field. If writers outnumber readers, that field is already wrong.
Open your quickstart and count the choices it presents before the reader's first success. Each one is extraneous load at the worst possible moment.
Point it at a real library's documentation. Yours, or an open-source project's. Count the unmarked fragments; in most corpora it is most of the samples, and that count is the finding.
Find a published per-request latency for a service you use and work out whether it is compute-only. If the batch size is not stated next to it, it is.
Check your README's claims against reality. Mine said 72 tests and there were 119, and nothing had ever checked, which is the cheapest class of defect there is.
Point the linter at a quickstart you own. Pipe-to-shell and credential literals are both common enough that you will probably find one.
Run the golden path. The before-and-after on one page, measured at the chunk level, is the demonstration and it takes five minutes to show.
Write the paragraph that states the resolution order and names the intuition it violates. It is the page that does not exist.

Write the tool descriptions twice. Once as "filter by kind", once as the guidance version, and connect it to a real client to see whether the filter choices change. That is a small experiment nobody does.
Classify twenty real content tasks on the two axes. An hour. The output is a table you can show, and the "never" rows are the interesting part.
Write a ten-term glossary for a corpus you already have, and run the measurement. The first number is almost always worse than the team's estimate, which is the point.
Run the vocabulary check and list the pages whose surface lacks their own readers' words. That list is a prioritised backlog nobody else has.
Measure your refusal rate. If you have any assistant over documentation, count what fraction of answers are refusals. A rate near zero is the finding, and almost nobody has the number.
Run the golden path. Step 4 is the one to remember, because it contradicts the common warning about MDX.
Run the golden path. The docutils-versus-Sphinx comparison is the part nobody has actually executed.

Measure your own agreement with yourself. Label ten pages, wait a week, label them again blind, and count the disagreements. That number is your ceiling, and reporting it alongside a precision figure is unusual enough to be memorable.
Find the fact in your corpus that is copied the most times and single-source that one. Start with a version number or a prerequisite, not an explanation.
